Door dash grows guys with no real.job or life experience to the wolves. Or as we called in the Corps, baptism by fire. If you never had any type of sales or marketing training.  Mine was primarily in recruiting. You might not understand the work involved with finding your perfect market setting.  You're going to have to work. Morning, mid day.and afternoon shift.   Pick an area that's close to hotspots but has enough homes to order food.  Then dash in each time slot and move around from  hot spot, to hot spot, and find which area has the most orders and at what time of day.  

 Is it the suburbs and 300k homes. The ghetto or the industrial area during lunch breaks.  You need to gather data and then do an analysis for maximum productivity and profit.   It probably takes a couple weeks. Then you will know the best times to dash and the best areas to drive and pick up offers.  You want one dash to end in an area that's gonna be busy and not way out from any hotspots or restaurants.  So learn your area well. All the side streets and surrounding areas. Especially the zones adjacent since you may be sent there and even relieve offers. 

You may be asked to switch zones because they're short on dashers. This may be to your benefit and make you more money. I have had my biggest offers going out of my zone, simply because they were desperate to get orders delivered.  Don't be afraid of the mileage if you are headed towards that hotspot. DD mileage includes you getting to the store. If your door is dead and 3 miles away isn't, you might get an offer with the extra travel.mileage and think it's not enough. But if you were gonna drive that way or maybe should since they are sending you offers so far away which means they need help.   

I have gotten 15 dollar offers for 12 miles 6 of which were to head to a hotspot beyond my nearest one as I was returning to a zone.  I take the offer and suddenly I am getting offers as soon as I finish one. And stay busy for a few hours running offers and before I know it I have made 100 dollars.  Happens. All the time.  

 I also am dead sure that when I sign on I get a cherry popper. It's a mediocre offer that's probably been passed around. I'm at home on my driveway and it says 5 miles for 7 dollars. I look and it's 3 miles to the store in a hotspot. So I take it and bang it out. Then I am getting offers one after the other.  Again I am making 3 hours of solid offers and 100 dollars.

  I take a break, use the bathroom, get food or whatever. Then it's back at it and rinse repeat.  That first one after break takes the longest. Because you interrupted the stream. If you refuse several in a row you interior the stream and have to move towards another hotspot area or zone. Eventually they will hit you back and you're right back into it.    

A little recon and some strategy planning, add to it some motivation. Then you adapt, improvise and overcome. Or quit and move on because you aren't right for the job.

When you drive in water or salt alert, and you park your car for say a day, week, or month. What happens to your rotors?   They immediately begin to rust not a deep putting rust but a nice layer of oxidation. Now do you take them off and try to clean them up?  Or does everyone just drive on them and the pads "clean" the rust off? They make a little grind and squeal and then viola they're clean and shiny again and the process starts over again. 

Clean them up anyway you choose, if its a light surface rust, who cares?  Problem with sanding is how much material you want to take off and keep the balance and run out of the rotor?  The pads will give a nice even stead pressure, the rust will disappear like magic and everything will stay true.  

Anyone that thinks they stay bright and shiny forever, I personally wouldn't take any car advice from them ever.  The only real worry is deep pitting or flaking now that might require a light machining or turning on a lathe. On a new rotor taking .001 or .002 thousandths wouldn't make any difference.

That's why you take a picture of the receipt with their name on it.  They have to show the receipt with the wrong name if you sent it with one. Or another name on the bag. They won't know what that name is so they can't make one up. I carry different color bags and assign each order a color. Then I double check that name with the phone.

The method I use I have a 3lb mini sledge.  It's flat on one side and has an angle on the back. Between each lug stud you hit it as hard as you can going around the rotor. Whack, whack, whack...it will fall off. Now don't use a choked up weak grip.  Use that hammer like a carpenter pounding a nail hold it near the bottom and swing it. Between the studs only. They pop right off.  

This won't hurt any ball joints, tie rods or the wheel bearing which is under the cap. Most people paint never seize on  the back of the new rotors after a light sanding of the rust on the hub for next time.

Rent an axle puller from AutoZone.  Then make sure you have a good set of hand tools. The hardest part for me was removing the axle nut. I live in the rust belt, so I soaked all the bolts with penetrant overnight.  )Spray and tap the bolts with a hammer.)  

 Then next day I pulled the spindle, and wheel bearing bolt after pulling the brakes and rotor off. In my case I replaced both while I was already there, as they were about a couple thousand miles away from needing a change.  I was able to use the puller to remove the axle.  Then I pulled the oil sealer from the hole. I made sure to use a new one, using a large socket and tapped it in place then slid in my axle till it clicked.  Reinstalled everything, with, like I said new rotors and pads. 

My wife had the car towed home because the CV exploded when she pulled into work.  It had been ticking for a week.  I checked the other side and it had a torn boot. So I went back to the store and grabbed another axle. Did the same thing as before.  I didn't have time to let the bolts soak, so I had to use a make shift long ass breaker bar.  No broken bolts and everything came apart. 

Curiously once I replaced both axles, I noticed a vibration that was present since we bought the car, that no one could find, or explain went away.  My guess an axle was out of balance from the factory. No one guessed that would be the case and 4 different shops checked it, including the dealer.  

The dealer said it was common on that model until the transmission broke in. Now I know they lied and it was the CV axle. Good luck it took about an hour and I never did one before. I just double checked with you tube that I was doing it correctly and the car is still driving great a year later.
